De Saint-Michel à Côte-des-Neiges, on pe: From Saint-Michel to Côte-des-Neiges, you can hear expressions like “kespass,” “renceur” or “c’est la hess” on the streets of Montréal. These terms are part of the everyday speech of the city’s youth, especially those from the neighbourhoods. This slang, made up mainly of a mix of English, French, Creole and Arabic, is increasingly criticized by Quebec politicians as contributing to the decline of French.
Dans une <l1>publicité publiée le 15 mar: In an <l1>ad published on March 15 by the Ministry of the French Language</l1>, the Legault government sounded the alarm about the use of a dialect spoken mainly by young Montrealers. The ad refers to the decline of the French language in Quebec and calls on Quebecers to reverse the trend. On April 21, people could see on TikTok and Instagram that a new restaurant was opening its doors: 514 Burger. Located on Saint-Laurent Boulevard, the snack bar offers a menu inspired by Montréal slang. On site, you can try dishes like the “pozzer,” the “czi” or other “bhy gyu.” Reactions to the 514 Burger menu have been mixed. La Converse therefore decided to welcome a group of Montrealers to discuss the importance and the nuances of the history of Montréal slang. A dialogue begins between students and people who helped popularize this slang.
C’est par un mercredi de mai que cette d: This discussion begins on a Wednesday in May. The day is winding down, and the last rays of sun are disappearing as the La Converse studio space welcomes its guests. The theme of the evening? The language experience in Montréal or, more precisely, the experience of the city’s slang.
Lorsque questionnées sur ce qui caractér: When asked what characterizes slang in Montréal, the people gathered around the table all answer the same thing: much of what is said in Montréal is borrowed from Haitian Creole. Shreez, a Laval rapper of Haitian origin, even exclaims: “Three quarters of the Creole dictionary is used in Montréal slang!” A few approving laughs can be heard in the room. Picking up on that, Carl-Henry, a student from Saint-Léonard originally from Haiti, says that “the melting pot is the best way to explain how we live; we’re not just in diversity, we mix, we all live together – it goes further than that.” He joins his two hands together to illustrate his point.
« La diversité est le mot qui décrit le: “Diversity is the word that best describes our city,” continues Izzy-S. A rapper born and raised in Saint-Michel, he proudly explains how his Haitian cultural heritage has enriched not only his lyrics, but also the spoken language of Montrealers. On the place of Creole in Montréal slang, however, he thinks it’s worth making a distinction: “Montréal Creole is unique, it’s not like what’s spoken in Haiti. For example, when you say something is giou, you’re not speaking Creole, because in Creole, we say gou. It’s not really Creole,” he explains.
À propos des expressions courantes que l: On the common expressions you can hear in Montréal, Houda, a social worker of Moroccan origin, shares an anecdote. “I work with newcomers,” she begins, “and many of them are young Haitians. Recently, while I was talking with one of them, he looked at me and interrupted me after I used the word soumoune (curious). He asked me how I knew that word, and I explained to him that certain Creole expressions were an integral part of the city’s slang.”
Quant aux Montréalais d’origine haïtienn: As for the Montrealers of Haitian origin in the room, they all agree that Montréal has taken Creole and adapted it to its own reality over the years, while blending in French and English expressions from here and elsewhere, thus creating a way of speaking true to the authenticity of its community.
Si certains voient dans l’utilisation du: While some see the use of Creole in the city’s slang as something negative, others prefer to see it as a form of love. That’s the case for Carl-Henry, who points out that being Haitian hasn’t always been “popular.” “In the 1970s, the Haitian community was treated very badly all over the world. When I think that those people could never have imagined that speaking their language would one day be seen as something popular, I find that extraordinary,” he exclaims. Izzy-S adds: “Before, being Haitian was hard. Now, I think it’s good that another culture embraces mine. When someone uses expressions in Creole, I see it as a form of love toward my culture.”
D’autres jugent néanmoins qu’il faut fai: Others nonetheless believe that nuance is needed in the use of Creole and Haitian culture. Houda doesn’t hesitate to say so. “I can’t speak on behalf of the Haitian community, but I think this applies to all communities. Wanting to be like Haitians today means forgetting to acknowledge all the history behind what is being said. People tell themselves: ‘Being Haitian is cool.’ They won’t look into the hidden history behind this culture. Being Haitian also comes with other forms of discrimination,” she says. And her point seems to be shared by everyone in the room. “Being Haitian is a fight. I’m Haitian and I’m proud that people are interested in my culture. We haven’t been here since yesterday, and the fact that we have an influence in the city, it has to be acknowledged,” adds Izzy-S.
« Je pense qu’il y a un manque de connai: “I think there’s a lack of knowledge about where the terms used in slang come from,” continues Houda. In her view, to truly embrace a culture, there has to be interest and a minimum of research beyond the act of appropriating words from the language. She points out that not everyone who uses slang is aware of the history tied to Haitian cultural identity. “The more popular it becomes, the more people will speak it. As a result, more and more people are using Creole expressions but have no idea about the history behind all of it,” she continues.
« À Montréal, on a une culture commune »: “In Montréal, we have a shared culture,” Sami, a young Montrealer of Algerian origin, chimes in. Having grown up between the Anjou neighbourhood and the city of Oran, Algeria, he says that “everyone in Montréal has brought something to Montréal culture.” “Haitians, North Africans, Latinos – we all made this culture look like us, and it gave us the beautiful city we live in! Like it or not, our cultures converge to give us Montréal culture.” Along the same lines, Carl-Henry speaks up. “What we have in Montréal is a unique phenomenon, it doesn’t exist anywhere else,” he says. “The way everyone here talks a bit like everyone else, it’s not something you’ll see elsewhere in the world. It’s a new reality. It’s normal that some people are more conservative about their culture,” he continues.
Si des gens comme Carl-Henry estiment qu: If people like Carl-Henry think a discussion is necessary, it’s not for nothing. And while unifying terms are sometimes used to describe the city of Montréal, that’s not always the case. The place different languages occupy in slang, and the very use of slang by many Montrealers, don’t always meet with unanimity. Rappers like Izzy-S and Shreez, who have both greatly helped widen the use of slang, say they aren’t bothered by it. “Young people are surrounded by this cultural identity. They listen to our music, hang out with other young people from different cultures: it’s normal that they speak slang. And it’s normal that they use expressions in Creole or Arabic, because it’s part of Montréal’s reality,” sums up Shreez.
En évoquant le fait que le slang soit gé: By pointing out that slang is generally used more by young people – that is, by Montrealers of Gen Z and Gen Y – the Fabreville rapper offers a different angle on the discussion. “I think the generation we belong to plays a role in how we see slang and what it implies,” says Carl-Henry. “I have a cousin a little older than me who grew up in the neighbourhoods in Montréal. He tells me that when he was young, Montréal was very different from what it is now. People from the neighbourhoods lived in a more dangerous city, they had different experiences. When they see that today some young people think it’s cool to talk like this, they react differently,” he says. He adds that since younger people are more comfortable with slang, they have a different relationship with it. Before, it was more problematic for certain reasons: people who lived in another Montréal therefore associate slang with more negative things.
Ayant grandi à Saint-Michel, Izzy-S ment: Having grown up in Saint-Michel, Izzy-S mentions that racism used to be much more present than it is today – in his neighbourhood and all over Montréal. “Racialized communities that experienced racism every day stuck together. Today, slang and its expressions don’t mean the same thing to them as they do to the new generations, who grew up in it,” he explains thoughtfully.
<strong>Il ne faut pas associer le slang: Slang shouldn’t be associated with the negative
« Ce n’est pas parce qu’on utilise ce sl: “Just because we use this slang doesn’t mean we’re less professional or less intelligent. We shouldn’t associate slang with the street and with what’s negative,” Houda says. The social worker believes Montréal slang is a richness and an asset rather than something shameful to hide. While she argues that the street and slang should be kept separate, Izzy-S wants to add some nuance to her words. “Just because it comes from the street and the neighbourhoods doesn’t mean it’s a bad thing,” he adds. “When we say it comes from the street, we’re referring to what’s said in the informal world, outside the professional world,” he continues.
Des gens comme Shreez ont tout de même r: People like Shreez have nonetheless managed to bring Montréal slang into their professional lives. “I rap the way I talk,” he says. “Actually, the way we talk in Montréal. When I go to France, I rap and talk the same way as I do here, because I want to show them where I’m from. I’m not going to change my accent to please people from elsewhere.” For Shreez, speaking local slang is a source of pride, and no one should be ashamed of it.
« Le slang de Montréal, ça m’a aidé à co: “Montréal slang helped me understand Quebec French,” Sami says. Having grown up between Algeria and Quebec, he says that, contrary to what’s said in the media, slang is not a threat to the French language. For him, it’s a plus, an extra. “Slang made it easier for me to integrate into Montréal. When I hear Montrealers use typically Arabic expressions, it makes me feel a little more at home,” he says.
Alors que plusieurs problématiques liées: As several issues tied to slang are raised, Carl-Henry brings up a subject that hasn’t yet been addressed in the conversation. “I feel like there’s starting to be a kind of disgust toward slang,” he says. “When we use it, it’s as if we’re associated with the bottom of society.” In the room, the young Montrealer’s reflection draws general approval. On slang’s bad reputation, Izzy-S replies: “It’s the same in every big city. Slang is always seen as something ratchet (crude, wretched), something associated with something bad, with a subculture.”
Houda, elle, souligne le bon côté de ce: Houda, for her part, highlights the good side of this informal way of speaking. “There’s still something comforting about slang,” begins the young woman, who grew up in Villeray. “When I meet someone who talks like me, it does something to me, I feel more connected to the person.” Carl-Henry, with an approving look, chimes in: “Slang is a marker of connection, it lets you feel at ease with others. When I meet people who speak the same dialect, it quickly brings us together. And they don’t need to be Haitian for us to understand each other, that’s what I find beautiful.”
<strong>« Moi, le slang, j’en suis fier: “Me, I’m proud of slang – it’s what unites us”
Carl-Henry estime qu’habiter à Montréal,: Carl-Henry believes that living in Montréal means, among other things, being able to do two things: distinguish the formal from the informal, and apply that distinction when communicating with others. “I’m a strong defender of Montréal slang,” he begins. “But you have to be able to do both. The problem is when some people aren’t able to switch.” He is alluding to code switching, that is, moving from one way of speaking to another depending on the context. “No matter where we live, we have to know how to tell casual language from formal language,” continues Izzy-S. “It’s not a problem unique to Montréal. Street language isn’t even written down, it isn’t regulated. They’re unwritten rules,” he says.
Alors que la soirée tire à sa fin, les p: As the evening draws to a close, the participants keep sharing in an exchange more animated than ever. Smiles form, and bonds take shape. By the end of the conversation, it’s clear that informal language has always existed and will keep existing. While modern slang grows more popular over time, many still wonder today about its place in an ideal French-speaking Montréal. “We have to start really embracing our culture. Me, I’m proud of slang – it’s what unites us,” Izzy-S concludes. Everyone then feels a little more at ease, a little more themselves and a little more Montrealer.
